name: Churches and Faith Organisations
blurb: Sermon prep, administration, and pastoral limits across hundreds of thousands of congregations, from Barna research and faith-tech platforms to Notre Dame ethics work.

points.desc: Census BTOS covers religious and civic organisations within its service-sector series; no better official measure exists yet, and this page says less rather than guessing.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.desc: The research firm's State of the Church work quantitatively tracks AI adoption, perception, and use among US congregations and ministry leaders - the closest thing to sector-wide survey data.
points.name: Barna Group runs the national studies

summary: No single body tracks AI adoption across America's hundreds of thousands of congregations - coverage comes from research firms, faith-tech platforms, and academic institutes, and this page names them rather than pretending a census exists. Sermon research, translation, accessibility, and administration are the working uses; every tradition is writing its own guidance.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Business Outlook Survey tracks religious organizations within its broader "Other services" category under NAICS 81, where 12.6% of firms reported using AI in the most recent period, up from 11.3% in the prior period. This figure covers a wide range of service businesses alongside religious organizations, so it should be read as a rough indicator rather than a precise measure of church-specific adoption. No dedicated official survey of AI use within congregations alone currently exists, and the Hartford Institute for Religion Research, which has a 45-year history of surveying congregational life, represents one of the few bodies positioned to produce that kind of granular data.

Within congregations, the clearest picture of how AI is actually being used comes from Gloo, the sector's primary technology platform, which serves thousands of US churches and builds AI tooling specifically for ministry contexts. Gloo describes its offering as values-aligned AI providing inference, retrieval-augmented generation, and assistant workflows, alongside knowledge graphs and data integrations designed to give ministry leaders holistic organizational insights. The platform frames AI deployment around what it calls "missional intelligence," covering administration, workflow automation, and custom model development tailored to faith-based organizations. Barna Group, a Christian research organization whose State of the Church work tracks adoption and perception among US congregations and ministry leaders, offers the closest thing to sector-wide survey data on how pastors and lay leaders are actually engaging with these tools.

Sermon preparation and scriptural interpretation appear to be a live concern at the pastoral level. Per Barna Group, nearly all pastors worry AI could misread scripture, and new Barna research shows most pastors want AI to present every interpretation of a difficult passage rather than settle on one. This finding points to a specific and recurring deployment question: whether AI can be trusted as a research or drafting aid for religious content without distorting doctrinal meaning or flattening interpretive diversity. It also signals a governance posture among clergy that is cautious rather than dismissive, interested in bounded rather than autonomous AI use.

The ethical framing around AI is more developed in this sector than formal adoption metrics might suggest. AI and Faith, an interfaith nonprofit, convenes technologists, theologians, academic researchers, and ethicists with the explicit goal of bringing faith-based moral frameworks into the broader AI ethics conversation. The organization notes that 85 percent of the world's population claims a religious affiliation, and it argues that the world's religions offer accumulated wisdom that should shape how AI is developed and used, addressing concerns around control, privacy, bias, economic well-being, and the nature of human identity. The University of Notre Dame's Institute for Ethics and the Common Good similarly funds interdisciplinary research on AI's impact on faith and human formation, including through a project called DELTA, which examines human formation in the age of AI.

For a leader at a congregation or faith-based organization considering deployment, the available evidence suggests that administrative and workflow uses carry the least institutional friction, while any AI involvement in scriptural interpretation, pastoral care, or theological content will encounter genuine and widely shared hesitation among clergy. Gloo's values-aligned model framework and its evaluation benchmarks tied to human flourishing dimensions represent the most developed sector-specific vendor response to that concern. The ethics infrastructure around this sector, from AI and Faith to Notre Dame's research programs, is active and organized, meaning that norms and guidance are being developed even if formal regulation is not yet in view.
